title: Local computation of MIS with polynomial degree dependence — resolved
formal: Does there exist a randomized local computation algorithm which, for every n-vertex simple undirected graph of maximum degree at most Δ, answers whether any requested vertex belongs to one consistently chosen maximal independent set, using at most C(Δ+1)^a(log(n+1))^b graph probes per answer? Here C,a,b are absolute constants, and with probability at least 1−1/n all n answers are jointly correct and meet the probe bound. The answer is yes, by Ghaffari’s FOCS 2022 result.
definitions: Take n≥2, vertex names [n], and 0≤Δ≤n−1, with n and Δ supplied. A probe (u,i), for u∈[n] and 1≤i≤Δ+1, returns u’s i-th neighbor in a fixed arbitrary ordering, or a null symbol if i exceeds its degree. The input is static; no preprocessing may inspect the graph for free. The algorithm can probe any vertex name, not only neighbors of the requested vertex. It uses shared randomness fixed independently of the graph, and its answer for a vertex is independent of the order, repetition, or presence of other vertex requests. With that randomness fixed, let I be the set of vertices receiving answer 1. Success requires that no edge has both endpoints in I and every vertex outside I has a neighbor in I. Local computation between probes is not charged here. The probability is over the shared randomness, for each fixed graph; it must control all vertices simultaneously. The original 2019 question uses one whole-neighbor-list query as its unit. The two access conventions differ by at most a factor Δ+1, so they have the same polynomial-in-Δ target.
answer_criterion: A globally consistent algorithm with the stated polynomial probe bound answers the historical question affirmatively; such an algorithm is now known. A bound averaged over a uniformly random requested vertex would not have sufficed. Optimizing the polynomial exponent is a further question, not an unresolved part of the existence statement retained here.
context:
A maximal independent set can contain a linear number of vertices. In a large implicit graph, a user may need only the membership of one vertex and have no reason to generate the entire set. An LCA supplies that membership on demand. Different answers must nevertheless describe one valid global solution: independently choosing a convenient set for each request could select both endpoints of an edge.

The target is maximality under inclusion, not maximum cardinality. A globally run greedy algorithm already computes a maximal independent set efficiently. The local difficulty is reconstructing the requested decision without following a chain of dependencies through a large part of the graph. Reusing fixed randomness allows separate requests to refer to the same implicit computation.

The degree dependence is central. A bound with an exponent growing as log log Δ is much larger than a fixed polynomial when Δ grows. The 2019 workshop question asks to remove that growing exponent while keeping dependence on n polylogarithmic. Its archived wording still presents this as an open question.

The 2022 algorithm resolves that target by carefully limiting which parts of a randomized distributed computation must be explored. Directly expanding a whole neighborhood for every simulated round is too expensive; controlling the actual dependencies is what permits a fixed polynomial in Δ. The remaining sparse components can then be completed consistently.

This resolved card stays in the catalogue to correct the inherited status and preserve its history. It also provides a useful reference point for more demanding targets, such as a linear or quadratic dependence on Δ. Those strengthen the question and should receive their own precise formulation and source if included.
why: Historically this asked whether a basic graph symmetry-breaking task can be answered locally with efficient dependence on both degree and graph size. Its resolution is fundamental to the LCA model and supports local algorithms for matching, coloring, and related problems.

importance.reason: A central historical efficiency question for local computation and consistent implicit graph solutions. It is resolved and therefore placed after unresolved candidates; the score records its significance rather than ongoing open status.

progress.text: The WOLA question records a Δ^(O(log log Δ)) polylog(n) bound and asks for poly(Δ,log n) probes.

Ghaffari’s Theorem 1.1 gives a polynomial-in-Δ per-vertex expected probe bound and a poly(Δ)·log(1/ε) tail bound with failure probability ε. Choosing ε inverse-polynomial in n yields the desired simultaneous bound by a union bound.
The result appears at FOCS 2022. The theorem also supplies a version using only poly(Δ log n) random bits. It explicitly leaves optimization of the degree exponent as a further direction.
Individual review matches the theorem’s model and guarantee to the saved 2019 existence question. This record is marked resolved affirmatively instead of remaining in the open-problem selection.
